question: According to Wes Kao, why is sharing your point of view an effective way to manage up?
expected_points: Offer your own recommendation instead of asking your manager to solve the problem from scratch.
This gives your manager a concrete starting point and reduces their cognitive load.
Supporting your view with evidence demonstrates active, strategic thinking.
evidence_quote: You give them something to build off of and that reduces the amount of mental lift that they have to put forth.

sections.heading: It reduces your manager’s cognitive load
sections.content: Rather than asking your manager to define the problem, develop solutions, and tell you what to do, offer your recommendation and invite feedback—for example, ask where they see gaps or whether you are thinking in the right direction. That gives them something to build on and reduces the mental lift they must provide.

sections.heading: It demonstrates proactive, strategic thinking
sections.content: Sharing a point of view, backed by evidence when possible, shows you are actively thinking about the business, anticipating problems, and forming hypotheses rather than waiting for instructions. Kao stresses that you do not need a perfect answer: you can describe a recurring problem and what you think may be happening. When sharing a report, identify insights and takeaways instead of leaving that work entirely to your manager.

sections.heading: It brings your on-the-ground perspective into view
sections.content: You may have closer visibility into an issue than your manager does—for example, through customer contact, support tickets, or data-cleaning work. Speaking up shares those observations and insights the manager might otherwise miss. Kao says even junior employees can do this.
